content:
With the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple took its next step toward its long-ranged vision of turning the iPhone into a single slab of glass: placing the Face ID module beneath the display.

Doing this without letting the Face ID components show through the screen and without ruining display quality in that area takes some clever engineering…

Jony Ive once described the design vision for the iPhone as a single sheet of glass, earlier in the device's history. Even though he's since left the company, that goal has carried forward. Apple eventually wants to hide all the technology that takes up screen space — including Face ID and the front-facing camera — completely under the display.

The iPhone 18 Pro becomes the first to achieve the former, but it certainly wasn't easy. Face ID requires the TrueDepth module to both project and receive infrared light, and infrared cannot pass through display pixels.

Apple had to create gaps between the pixels large enough for the infrared light to pass through, without noticeably degrading the screen quality. To do this, the company's engineers set out to design a brand-new pixel arrangement that spaces the pixels farther apart without affecting the display.

iFixit showed off this pixel arrangement under a microscope, and Apple confirmed to me that the overall pixel density in that module area has been cut in half. This could have created a second problem: the halved pixel density could have made that part of the screen noticeably dimmer, so Apple compensated by making those pixels brighter. The components also seem to include infrared filters to block visible light from passing through, further hiding the components beneath.

The result is astonishing. In practice, even looking very carefully, it's almost impossible to spot the TrueDepth camera components. I tried macro photography at various screen colors and lighting conditions and still couldn't capture them. That's not to say they're completely undetectable — iFixit's microscope images prove they're there — but in daily use, you'll never notice them.

This allowed it to make the Dynamic Island smaller, which in turn lets the iPhone display three Live Activities simultaneously, one more than before. In some future iPhone, the front-facing camera will also be hidden under the display. The technology to do this exists, but the image quality trade-offs are still beyond what Apple is willing to accept. It's a matter of when this gets solved, not if.
